title: Moffat County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Moffat County wells have a 217 ft median depth and 8 gpm median yield. See local drilling costs, water levels, and well risks before you buy.
h1: Water wells in Moffat County, Colorado
intro_html:
Moffat County wells are all over the map, from very shallow alluvial holes along creek bottoms to deep fractured-bedrock wells out in the sagebrush. Before you buy land or plan a new home here, it helps to know how deep most wells go, how much water they typically make, and what that means in real drilling dollars.

The numbers below come from 4,333 Colorado Division of Water Resources permits in Moffat County. They give a realistic picture of depth, yield, water levels and drilling activity across the county, from the Craig area out toward Maybell and Dinosaur.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Moffat County
sections.html:
Across Moffat County, reported well depths center around a 217 ft median. Half of the wells with depth data fall between 73 and 360 ft, so most domestic and stock wells end up somewhere in that range. A small share push much deeper, with the 90th percentile at 500 ft and one recorded well down to 4,100 ft.

Depths are spread out: about 29% of wells are under 100 ft, 34% run 100–300 ft, 31% are 300–600 ft, and roughly 6% go past 600 ft. That mix tells you bids need to allow for both shallow alluvial completions near drainages and significantly deeper fractured-bedrock targets on higher benches and ridges.

In practice, a driller will look closely at nearby permits around Craig, Maybell or Dinosaur to tighten that depth estimate for your specific parcel before setting a price.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you actually get
sections.html:
Of the wells that report a pump test, the median yield in Moffat County is 8.0 gpm, with the middle half between 6.0 and 12.0 gpm. That’s plenty for a typical exempt household well and some outdoor use if you manage it sensibly.

The yield distribution is encouraging: 0% of reported wells are under 1 gpm, about 11% fall in the 1–5 gpm bracket, 70% land between 5–15 gpm, and 19% are 15+ gpm. In other words, most wells produce solid domestic-and-stock flows, with a minority on the low side.

Because almost all local wells tap unnamed fractured-bedrock rather than a nice uniform sandstone, yields can still vary a lot over short distances. Checking nearby permits on Colorado Well Finder is the best way to gauge risk for a particular lot.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Where static water level is reported, Moffat County wells show a median depth to water of 77 ft, with the middle half between 31 and 140 ft below ground. That gives you a rough idea of pumping lift and power needs once the well is built.

By decade, the median static level was about 80 ft in the 1980s, 65 ft in the 2000s, 82 ft in the 2010s, and 64 ft in the 2020s. Those ups and downs don’t point to a steady decline so much as normal variation from climate, measurement methods and where new wells were drilled.

Still, in fractured-bedrock systems, water levels can be very local. Plan your pump setting conservatively, especially if you’re on higher ground away from alluvial valleys.

sections.heading: Who’s been drilling here, and for what
sections.html:
Moffat County has a long drilling history. Only a handful of permits show up in the 1950s and 1960s, then activity jumps: 381 permits in the 1970s, 590 in the 1980s, and 820 in the 1990s. The 2000s record 659 permits, the 2010s have 490, and there are already 470 permits issued in the 2020s, with records running through 2026.

Domestic and household wells account for about 55% of permits, stock wells another 25%, with 3% for irrigation and 16% for monitoring. Almost all are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock, with smaller numbers in Alluvial or the Wasatch-Fort Union.

Local names that show up a lot in the records include Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 348 wells, Craig Drilling (Herod, James Leroy) with 267, and Visintainer Co. (Visintainer, Walter) with 251.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Moffat County
sections.html:
In the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground around Moffat County, typical drilling runs about $50–$75 per foot. At the county’s 217 ft median depth, that puts the borehole itself roughly in the $10,800–$16,300 range before any pump or plumbing.

Once you add a submersible pump, pressure tank, trenching, pitless adapter, and electrical work, a completed domestic well at that median depth usually falls around $16,800–$28,300 based on the same cost model. Deeper wells toward the 300–500 ft end of the local spread scale up quickly.

Site access, distance to the house, rocky conditions and winter drilling can all move you toward the high side of those numbers. A driller quoting off nearby wells around Craig, Maybell or Dinosaur will give the most realistic estimate.

sections.heading: Key risks: water quality, low yield and siting
sections.html:
Moffat County’s fractured-bedrock aquifers can be hit-or-miss. While reported yields look decent overall, there is still a real chance of an underperforming well, especially up on higher benches. A careful look at nearby permits and test data is your best protection against surprises.

On the water quality side, state mapping shows about 68 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 33 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles. That doesn’t mean your specific well is contaminated, but it does make professional water testing important before you rely on it for drinking.

Plan well and septic separation properly, keep the well uphill from leach fields where you can, and pay attention to local setbacks when laying out a new build.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well in Moffat County
sections.html:
For an existing home on a well, ask for the well permit, any drill log, and recent water-quality tests. With a county median yield of 8.0 gpm and most reported wells between 6.0 and 12.0 gpm, many systems are fine for normal household use, but you still want proof of performance.

On vacant land, pull up nearby permits on Colorado Well Finder for depth, yield and static level. In a county where depths run from under 100 ft to 600+ ft, that local pattern will drive your real drilling budget.

Talk with a driller early about siting the well relative to power, the house pad, and septic. In over-appropriated basins you may also hear about augmentation plans, so check your specific water-rights situation before you stake everything on a new well.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Moffat County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on reported data, the median well depth in Moffat County is about 217 ft, with half of wells between 73 and 360 ft. Roughly 29% are under 100 ft, 34% fall in the 100–300 ft range, 31% are 300–600 ft, and about 6% go deeper than 600 ft. Local geology and elevation around your parcel will push you toward one end of that spread.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Moffat County?
faq.a: For wells that report pump tests, the median yield in Moffat County is 8.0 gpm, and the middle half are between 6.0 and 12.0 gpm. About 11% of wells come in between 1–5 gpm, 70% are in the 5–15 gpm range, and 19% produce 15+ gpm. That’s generally adequate for household and stock use, but always verify the specific well you’ll be relying on.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Moffat County?
faq.a: In Moffat County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, drilling typically runs about $50–$75 per foot. At the local median depth of 217 ft, that translates to roughly $10,800–$16,300 for the borehole. A complete domestic setup with pump, tank, trenching and electrical usually ends up around $16,800–$28,300 at that depth, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping in Moffat County?
faq.a: Reported static water levels don’t show a clear long-term decline. Median depth to water was about 80 ft in the 1980s, 65 ft in the 2000s, 82 ft in the 2010s, and 64 ft in the 2020s. Those shifts likely reflect climate swings and where wells were drilled, rather than a steady drop. Conditions are still very local, so check recent nearby wells for the best picture.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Moffat County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well. County mapping shows about 68 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 33 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles, which means some localized risks exist. Many private wells test clean, but you should always do a full water-quality test—especially for PFAS and metals—before using a well as your main drinking-water source.
